subtopic: MR. PERRON-SYSTEM OF CALLING LIBERAL MEMBERS FOR VOTES IN COMMITTEE
MR. PERRON-SYSTEM OF CALLING LIBERAL MEMBERS FOR VOTES IN COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which deals with equal rights and prerogatives for all members of this house.
The following facts show that there is discrimination, since some hon. members enjoy a privilege which is denied to others:
When the Speaker is in the Chair, and a vote is called, we know that bells ring in every parliament building to warn hon. members. However, when the house is sitting in committee of the whole there are no bells nor any other means to notify members who are in their offices.
It seems that the government has installed for the use of the Liberal members only, a warning system commonly called "electric buzzer" which notifies every Liberal member in his office so he may hurry to the house and vote. This privilege is for Liberal members only and not for members of the other political parties.
Consequently, it would be appropriate to know:
1.	Who paid for the installation of that system in Liberal members' offices?
2.	Why was this done for Liberal members only?
3.	Who instructed that such a system be installed for Liberal members only?
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Rondeau), that this matter be referred to the Speaker, and that the Speaker report to the house as to which
steps should be taken to remedy this situation.

I have reason to believe that is not so but I must, of course, check this statement and see whether it is factual. Therefore, without rendering any decision at the moment I should like to check the facts on this matter and take them into consideration.

maintopic: MR. FAIRWEATHER-RESPONSIBILITY FOR CUSTODY OF LUCIEN RIVARD
MR. FAIRWEATHER-RESPONSIBILITY FOR CUSTODY OF LUCIEN RIVARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question of privilege.
On March 3, 1965 the Minister of Justice informed this house that the government had no responsibility for the safe custody and incarceration of Lucien Rivard, and that the safe custody of a prisoner charged with an indictable offence is exclusively a matter for the provincial authorities in whose jail the prisoner is confined during the judicial process.
The minister later publicly repeated this denial of responsibility over the facilities of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The last time he did so was last evening on a program called "News Magazine".
It is not denied by the Minister of Justice that under the provisions of section 13 of the Extradition Act, Rivard was arrested, held in custody, his application for habeas corpus heard, and was committed to prison as if charged and convicted of an indictable offence. Upon final disposition of the judicial process it was then the responsibility of the Minister of Justice, under our treaty obligations with the United States, to order the surrender and delivery of Rivard to United States authorities.
This parliament foresaw that by reason of the insecurity of any particular provincial prison there was a possibility of escape, and that the minister had a special duty to carry out the treaty obligations in respect of an extraditable prisoner. In such circumstances parliament, by statute, authorizes the governor in council to provide for the safe custody of every federal prisoner confined in a provincial jail in certain circumstances. To this end this parliament provided in section 3 of the Prisons and Reformatories Act:
The governor in council or the lieutenant governor of the province may, if, from the insecurity or unfitness of any gaol of any county or district for the safe custody of prisoners, or for any other cause, he deems it expedient so to do, order any person charged with an indictable offence confined in such gaol, or for whose arrest a warrant has been issued, to be removed to any other place for safekeeping, or to any gaol, which place or gaol shall be named in such order, there to be detained until

discharged in due course of law, or removed for the purpose of trial to the gaol of the county or district in which the trial is to take place.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice has misinformed this house and continues to misinform parliament and the country by his failure to correct this misstatement as to the duty imposed upon him and upon the governor in council by section 3 of the Prisons and Reformatories Act and the sovereign power given by this parliament to the governor general in council to assume, upon the minister's recommendation, safe custody of a prisoner.
I suggest the minister has danced a constitutional minuet in respect of this whole affair, bowing grandly to the attorney general of Quebec as he casually divested himself of any responsibility for seeing to it that special arrangements were made to suit the very special circumstances of this case.
The minister's narrow concept of "special arrangements" is manifested by his often repeated statement that he could not post members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police outside every provincial prison. Such a silly proposition could only be conceived of by the minister; no one else has ever made any such suggestion. Neither the minister nor the government has given the house any evidence to think otherwise than that the minister never once communicated with anyone in Quebec requesting that extra precautions should be taken to ensure the custody of Rivard.
Mr. Speaker, Favreau's follies may be the newest and most zestful of Canadian musical comedies of the spring season, but I for one do not think it is very funny.

subtopic: PRODUCTION OF COIN SETS
PRODUCTION OF COIN SETS
speechtext:
1.	Is the number of coins to be put into circulation determined in advance and, if so, for what reason?
2.	Are Canadian requirements satisfied before release to the American market and, if not, for what reason?
3.	Would it be possible to give priority to Canadian collectors?
4.	For what reason did the mint cease production of coin sets prior to meeting all existing demand?

speakeroldname: Mr. L. T. Pennell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PRODUCTION OF COIN SETS
speechtext:
1. The number of coins to be put into circulation cannot be determined in advance. The demand for coins for circulation is determined by the public, and the mint does its best to meet the full demand. The number of coin sets to be prepared and sold to collectors and others is determined by the production facilities available, as well as the demand.
2.	The main requirements for Canadian coin are for circulation in Canada and these are normally satisfied in full. The sale of numismatic sets has never been restricted to Canadian buyers and cannot be effectively restricted to such buyers.
3.	It would not be possible effectively to give priority to Canadian collectors. Genuine collectors in Canada could not be distinguished from those buying to sell to others, including persons outside Canada, without intensive and expensive investigation, which would be very annoying to those ordering sets. Moreover, discrimination against buyers outside the country of origin would no doubt be resented by Canadian numismatists who

Questions
desire to collect uncirculated coin from other countries.
4.	As announced by the Minister of Finance on February 1, 1965, the mint will produce 1965 coin sets until all orders have been filled. Public notice will be given as soon as it is possible to deal with new orders or with those received in January and returned to senders.

subtopic: EXPROPRIATION OF APARTMENT SITE, OTTAWA
speechtext:
1. (a) The national capital commission sought authority in a submission to the treasury board on 27 January, 1965 for this expropriation. Order in council authority was granted to the commission on 19 February 1965.
(b) Reason for this expropriation is as follows: "The government has decided that a new headquarters building for the Department of National Defence should be located in Lebreton Flats. The outline plan being prepared by architects collaborative for the redevelopment of Lebreton Flats, while not yet complete, has indicated that the best site for the headquarters building for the Department of National Defence would be on the eastern side of the Flats, about 100 yards from the escarpment. It will be the largest and therefore the most significant building architecturally in the area.
The new city zoning by-law would permit a building of some 150 feet to be built on the escarpment, which is some 60 feet higher than the ground level in Lebreton Flats. The commission believed that if a tall building were erected on the escarpment it would detract from the plans for the redevelopment of Lebreton Flats. It therefore believed that this site should be acquired so that the government could be sure that a building will be erected on this site as part of and in harmony with the development of the ad-

Questions
jacent area. It would moreover contribute to the over-all government development from parliament hill westward through the Leb-reton Flats and along the Ottawa river parkway."
2.	The national capital commission is not authorized to expropriate any property without the authority of the governor in council.
The commission is therefore unable to announce an expropriation until such authority is given to it. If the commission were to indicate it intended to seek authority to expropriate properties, this would affect their value, and if authority to expropriate were not given, the owners would have cause to complain about the actions of the commission.
3.	The national capital commission cannot make payments to a municipal authority for what may be considered to be anticipated losses. The city is paid a grant equivalent to full property taxes for departmental and crown agency buildings of the federal government except those buildings used for educational, religious or charitable purposes.
The acquisition of property by the crown is part of the normal redevelopment of the city of Ottawa. It is no different from the activities of private developers where they remove obsolete buildings from various sites and re-erect new buildings. When the government removes a building, there may be a loss of tax revenue on the building itself, although grants in lieu of taxes on the vacant land being held for construction of government administrative buildings are still paid. However, any loss is more than offset by the revenues from other government buildings being erected and brought into use elsewhere. The total assessment on government properties in the city of Ottawa increased from $105,279,875 in 1960 to $116,298,675 in 1963.

I come back to the subject matter. First of all, it is a very important matter, since the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) yesterday offered a $15,000 reward for the apprehension of Lucien Rivard. But, last Saturday, federal, provincial and municipal police officers received a list of houses they should visit in order to arrest Lucien Rivard. The name of the first person on that list, that is the person to be visited in the first place, happened to be the name of a Montreal M.L.A.
Five minutes before the detectives left for that series of searches, a secret telephone call was received at the office of the detectives and police forces from a political personality requesting, even demanding the cancellation of the visit of police bodies at the home of that M.L.A. whose name was on top of the list in the hands of the police bodies.
I therefore submit that there was a pernicious intervention by political personalities with a view to hindering the police bodies and forces from carrying out a house search which was considered as being the first one and a must on the list held by the police forces. They did not call at the home of that M.L.A. following a secret telephone call from some influential political personality at five minutes to five in the morning, that is five minutes before the police force left to undertake that series of house searches.
That is why I will be asking during this urgent debate: who made that telephone call at the very last minute, who asked and ordered that no search be made at the home of that M.L.A.? Who made that telephone call? Why and under what authority were the police kept from raiding the house of that person heading the list of those to be visited in an effort to find Lucien Rivard?
So, I say it is most important, and I emphasize these words, it is most important to discuss that political interference on the part of this government, and this matter is also most urgent, since the Minister of Justice stated that a reward would be offered after an unusual delay. I suppose the unusual delay to find Lucien Rivard has expired, since a reward has been offered and an abnormal delay has elapsed.
I suggest it is urgent that police forces have a free hand and can act without hindrance from political authorities or personalities, that they be free to recapture Lucien


Rivard. Last Monday morning police were prevented from doing their job.
That is why I say it is most important to bring politicians to reason and to see to it that police authorities have the necessary discretion to do their work according to their judgment and their conscience.

I deal with this exclusively from a procedural point of view, and direct Your Honour's attention to citation 181 in Beauchesne's fourth edition, which establishes the rights of members to answers and the traditional rights of ministers in their replies:
A minister may decline to answer a question without stating the reason for his refusal, and insistence on an answer is out of order, no debate being allowed. A refusal to answer cannot be raised as a question of privilege, nor is it regular to comment upon such refusal.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS FROM MEMBER FOR DOLLARD RESPECTING VINCENT COTRONI
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, this motion asserts that a number of documents exist and asks for their production by the government.
I should like to deal first with the request for documents submitted to the parole board in the case of one Vincent Cotroni of Montreal. It is true that representations have been made to the parole board with respect to Mr. Cotroni, but it seems to me that the work of the parole board would be completely nullified if documents or other information from its files, much of which would only be given on a confidential basis, became subject to production in parliament. For that reason I hope there will be no desire on the part of the hon. member to insist on this motion for the production of such documents.
Next, in respect of the point of order, there were only two documents which came to me

Inquiries of the Ministry or to the Department of Justice regarding this man. The main one was a petition from Cotroni himself, addressed to the governor in council and submitted by Cotroni's solicitor. I did not feel that the granting of Cotroni's request should be recommended to my colleagues and I so indicated to his solicitor.
The other document was a letter to me relating to Cotroni's request.
Again in respect of the point of order, there is no correspondence whatever between Andre Letendre, my executive assistant, and Mr. Guy Rouleau, M.P., regarding Cotroni, notwithstanding the assertion made in the motion that such correspondence exists, nor is there any letter to anyone from Mr. Rouleau on the subject. The assertion in the motion, as hon. members will have noticed, has given rise to regrettable publicity damaging to a member of this house and to a public servant. In the circumstances I hope the hon. member will see fit to drop this motion.

maintopic: REPRESENTATIONS FROM MEMBER FOR DOLLARD RESPECTING VINCENT COTRONI
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the evasive manner in which the Minister of Justice has treated this motion I would ask the house to allow it to stand for a week, so I can give it some consideration after I have read Hansard.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STEPS TO STABILIZE PRICE LEVELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance which relates to the recent announcement that the cost of

Inquiries of the Ministry living index rose during the month of February and has now reached the all-time high of 137.2. In view of the fact that since these figures were compiled there have been increases in the prices of steel, lumber and other commodities, and in view of the fact that one of the goals set by the economic council of Canada was that the government should endeavour to obtain some stability in price levels during the next five-year period, in respect of which Professor Deutsch suggested that the government ought to take immediate steps toward implementing this as quickly as possible, would the minister indicate what steps he proposes to deal with this situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STEPS TO STABILIZE PRICE LEVELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend and I were most privileged this morning to hear a brief presented by the Canadian Labour Congress, during the course of which the congress expressed the view that there was no immediate danger of inflation. At that time I thought my hon. friend agreed with them, but perhaps I was wrong.
Like all members of this house I regret any increase in the cost of living, but I would point out to my hon. friend that during the last 12 months, to the end of February, the consumer price index in Canada has gone up by 2 per cent which, with the exception of the United States increase, is the smallest increase of any of some 10 or 11 countries including Germany, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Sweden, Japan, France, Belgium, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Italy. While I regret any increase, I think we can take some satisfaction from the fact that the increase which has occurred in Canada is lower than that of any of the other countries I have mentioned.
My hon. friend has asked what we intend to do about this situation. I think the first thing we must do is to define the extent of the problem. As I have just said, I felt that my friend applauded this morning the statement made by the congress, a very influential group, that in their opinion this was not one of the major problems with which we have to contend.

subtopic: STEPS TO STABILIZE PRICE LEVELS
speechtext:
I have a supplementary question. Instead of answering my question the minister seems to have posed a dilemma for himself. I would be interested in reading any statement of the Canadian Labour Congress to the effect that they are not concerned about the rising costs of living. On


the contrary, they devoted one entire section of their brief to a request to the government to do something about the increased price of steel.

subtopic: STEPS TO STABILIZE PRICE LEVELS
speechtext:
Order, please. I wonder
whether the hon. member will pose his question.

subtopic: STEPS TO STABILIZE PRICE LEVELS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the minister's statement that the first thing we have to do is obtain information, I should like to ask him whether he proposes to take any steps to ascertain whether the increases in the price of steel, lumber and other commodities were warranted and, in the event they are not, what action does the government propose to take to deal with the situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: STEPS TO STABILIZE PRICE LEVELS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to assure my hon. friend that I was not seeking to confront myself with a dilemma, but attempting to confront my hon. friend with a dilemma. This whole situation is being considered by the government and I hope that we will be able to make a statement before very long.

subtopic: STEPS TO STABILIZE PRICE LEVELS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question and I suggest the urgency of it can be found in the fact that over 25 per cent of the Canadian population belongs to the fixed income group. Does the hon. minister feel that his statement will satisfy the 35 per cent of our population living in poverty, deprivation and destitution, all of whom must pay these increasing costs from their fixed and shrinking incomes?

subtopic: STEPS TO STABILIZE PRICE LEVELS

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 8 the hon.
Inquiries of the Ministry member for Edmonton West inquired about the labour negotiations affecting the staff of Expo '67. I have now received a report from the exhibition corporation to the effect that these negotiations have been completed to what appears to be the satisfaction of the staff and the unions. There are at present some 152 positions in the corporation included in the bargaining unit. The two unions concerned, the Montreal labour council and the confederation of national trade unions, have agreed that these employees will be free to join or not join a union as they see fit. Effective March 10, however, new employees whose positions fall within the bargaining unit will be called upon to join either of the two unions as a condition of their employment with the corporation. Union dues will only be collected from those who will be members of unions.
Hon. members will be aware that the corporation has negotiated an agreement with the two labour councils in the Montreal area which provides for unionization of employees on the site of the exhibition in exchange for a no strike undertaking and consultative machinery to settle all grievances. I am happy to advise the house that all parties to the agreement are working together to apply it constructively and in the best interests of the exhibition.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Can the minister advise whether this is in conformity with government labour policy and was this settlement encouraged or proposed by the government?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. From the very outset, as hon. members will realize, it has been most desirable to reach an agreement with the labour unions in the area in which the exhibition will operate to avoid strikes. One of the besetting problems of the New York world's fair, for example, was the number of interruptions that took place, and it was very much in the interests of exhibitors and the three governments concerned that such an arrangement should be made. While the government was not the instigator, we think that the corporation has acted very wisely.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the joint committee considered this clause and made a recommendation with regard to what is called dropout. I am informed copies of the amendment are on the way to the chamber.

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF CONTRIBUTORY PROGRAM
speechtext:
In French and English. I move, seconded by my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue:
That subsection (3) of section 48 be amended by striking out lines 9 and 10 on page 37 and substituting the following:
(i)	15 per cent of the number so remaining, and
if such 15 per cent includes a fraction of a month
This amendment provides for the increase of the dropout allowance from 10 to 15 per cent. Hon. members will recall that the joint committee on the Canada pension plan had recommended an increase to 20 per cent, after having heard representations from the teachers federation, the firefighters association, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Labour Congress, Dr. Robert Clark and Professor McGregor, to the effect that 4.7 years were insufficient to allow for years of schooling beyond the age 18 and for periods of illness and unemployment which might occur before the age 65. A 20 per cent dropout, as recommended by the committee, would allow the total contributory period to be reduced from 47 to 37.6 years.
The government has given a great deal of consideration to the recommendation of the joint committee and to the views of those organizations which raised this matter in their representations before the committee. Subsequent to the hearings of the joint committee a brief was received from the students union but I believe it was not circulated to the members of the committee. It was a particularly good brief and it also recommended an increase in the percentage of dropout allowed.
It is apparent that some retirement plans have a normal retirement age lower than 65 years. Some may have 62 or 60 as a retirement age, and some even lower. While some

Canada Pension Plan
adjustment to account for these special circumstances appears to have some merit, it must be kept in mind that many of those covered by such plans continue working either in the same type of employment or in some other type of work.
In the case of teachers many continue on to age 65, even though their teachers retirement plans may be set at an age lower than 65. In the case of the firefighters many of these able-bodied men take on other employment after retiring from the firefighting service. None the less there is a valid point that some recognition of these special circumstances needs to be made.
At the other end of the scale are those who continue on in school beyond age 18. Some of these may be for only a year or two in high school and in technical and vocational schools, in which case the amount of dropout provision needed to compensate for this period is not great. But others continue on to university. In their case many work in the vacation period and earn enough more than the $600 basic minimum to be able to count such a year. A student who has earned, say, $800 in summer employment will contribute $3.60 for the year, that is, 1.8 per cent on $200, and will be credited with $800 in pensionable earnings. Also, for most of those who receive a university education average earnings will be well over the $5,000 earnings ceiling throughout their later careers. They will probably get a maximum benefit under the Canada pension plan, for they, it should be expected, will for most of their work life be above the income ceiling. Also, they will in most cases earn sufficient income to permit them to make substantial other provision for their retirement; and that of course includes private pension plans. Teachers, for example, as in the case of other groups such as civil servants, will have other retirement benefits from well established retirement plans. Also it is generally true that those with a university education would not require as large a dropout provision for unemployment as would industrial workers.
Having reviewed all these considerations, the government was of the view that somewhat more generous provision was needed by way of dropout; but the question was, how to achieve this and how much additional compensation should be provided. Any attempt to deal with individual groups by providing special dropout provisions raised so many administrative problems and anomalies affecting the equity of treatment of
fMiss LaMarsh.]
different groups in the population that it was decided an increase in the general dropout provision as proposed by the joint committee was the most practical and fairest way of achieving this objective.
When the joint committee made its recommendation it had only a general indication of the magnitude of the cost involved in any change. Since that time the chief actuary has been able to make estimates of the cost, and this has been of some assistance to the government in arriving at its decision. Two points should be emphasized. Raising the percentage of the dropout provision has no effect in the first ten years because it does not become operative during the transition period. It is of particular significance for only long term costs. A higher percentage not only makes the plan more generous for groups that have a shorter work career, such as those I have mentioned, but it makes the plan more generous for all participants. The low years or no years of earnings, or perhaps I should say the low months or no months of earnings, that can be dropped out are increased for all contributors under the plan.
On the assumption of an annual rate of increase in average earnings of 4 per cent, and on the basis of intermediate cost estimates, the chief actuary estimates that expenditures on benefits would be increased by the following amounts if a 20 per cent dropout rather than a 10 per cent dropout were adopted: For 1980, $12 million; 1985; $38 million; 1990, $76 million; 1995, $125 million; for the year 2000, $180 million; for the year 2005, $244 million. As I have pointed out, that would be the effect of doubling the dropout provision which appears in the present bill.
It will be noted that toward the end of this period the effects of that provision in increasing costs are very considerable. Reserve fund projections based on intermediate cost estimates, a 4 per cent annual rate of increase in earnings and accumulation interest rate of 5 per cent to the end of 1975, and 4 per cent thereafter, show a considerable effect on the reserve fund. Twenty years from now, in 1985, reserves would be $200 million less; five years later, in 1990, reserves would be $600 million less; in 1995 the reserve fund would be $1,300 million smaller. In the year 2000, assuming the present level of contributions, reserves would be down to $300 million with a 10 per cent dropout provision; but if it were increased to 20 per cent there would be a deficit of $2.1 billion. In the long term, the increase in total benefits resulting from

a change from a 10 per cent to a 20 per cent dropout provision would be equivalent to an increase of about 5 per cent in the required pay-as-you-go contribution rates.
In proposing the amendment to clause 48 (3) the government took into account the special circumstances of the groups which might be adversely affected by the dropout, and the long term effect on the finances of the plan. A dropout of 15 per cent, however, as is included in the government's amendment, will allow the contributory period of 47 years to be reduced to 40 years. It should be pointed out again that no one will be affected by the dropout provision in the first ten years of the plan, since the dropout allowance is not permitted to reduce one's contributory period below 120 months, or ten years. During this time anyone who can do so will want to contribute in order to build up the level of the benefit to which he is entitled. For the next ten years of the plan, from 1976 to 1986-that is, the second ten years-it makes only a very small difference whether the dropout provision is 15 per cent or 20 per cent. A dropout of 15 per cent by 1986 will allow three years of earnings to be removed from the calculation of one's average earnings, and a dropout of 20 per cent will allow four years of earnings to be removed from the calculation.
Thus it can be seen that it is only after the plan has been in operation for many years that the size of the percentage dropout takes on much significance. At that time a decision could be made regarding the appropriate level of the dropout allowance, having in mind the trends in employment that will have developed 20 years from now. Automation and other developments may affect the normal retirement age over the next decade or so, which will mean this provision will need to be reviewed periodically.
This is the kind of problem that the draftsmen and the advisory committee on the Canada pension plan would be expected to study very carefully as relevant information becomes available to it. No doubt the advisory committee would be in a position to make a recommendation to the government of the day for the appropriate level of the dropout allowance after a decade or two of experience with the operation of the Canada pension plan. In the meantime, Mr. Chairman, we consider that it would be prudent, as a government measure, for the committee to consider the adoption of a 15 per cent rather than a 20 per cent dropout provision as recommended by the special joint committee.

I understand very well the facetious remarks of the parliamentary secretary and forgive him, but he does not add one word to the debate we are undertaking.
As I say, there are three groups who would be affected. It was felt by some members in the committee that a dropout provision of 25 per cent was what was really required, because that would allow a student to continue in school until age 25 and then retire at some time before the age of 65 without losing out. However, others pointed out that 10 per cent was in the bill and therefore a compromise agreement was reached on 20 per cent, which is what the committee recommended. I assume that since the committee reported further estimates have been made; and the minister has pointed out that the actuarial result will reduce the fund at one point below the level it should be. However, we feel that the reduction in the dropout period from 20 per cent to 15 per cent will make even more important the problem for students. Because if you take the present 15 per cent dropout, from 47 years it allows a dropout period of seven years. In the proposal which will be made, of which notice has already been given, students up to the age of 25 years would not have their years of dropout counted. The years between 18 and 25 are now proposed to be the dropout period. Therefore I do not think that the amendment will meet the case of the students, as the minister attempted to show it would. It will mean that if they do continue on at school until they reach the age of 25 they will not be able to miss one further year in their whole lifetime earning period up to age 65, which will certainly not meet the situation for them. Neither will it meet the situation for the others who put forward a strong case to the committee.
The minister pointed out that the provision would not be applicable in the first 10 years; that between now and 10 years hence it does not matter whether the dropout period percentage is 10 per cent or 20 per cent or 25 per cent, it can still be amended at a later date. I merely ask this question: If it does not matter for the next 10 years, then why bother moving the amendment at all? It seems that if the amendment is to be made it should be made on a basis which will meet the situation. If at the end of the 10 year

period which the minister has mentioned it is found that the conditions of employment and business generally to which she referred have changed, then the reduction might be made the other way. It really seems unnecessary to make any amendments at all if the minister takes the attitude that it does not matter in any case.
I merely say, Mr. Chairman, that the increase to 15 per cent will not meet the situation for students, firemen, teachers and many other people who are forced into a shorter earning lifetime by the circumstances of their profession; and I must express great disappointment that the dropout period was not increased to the amount recommended by the joint committee. I have not discussed with my hon. friend from Perth whether we will support this amendment. I think 15 per cent is better than 10 per cent and perhaps we should be thankful that there has been some increase; but as I say, I am disappointed that the recommendation of the joint committee was not accepted.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is pretty well established that the member for Winnipeg North Centre has been one of the keen supporters of this measure and has done everything he can to further its progress. However, I regret I must express very keen disappointment at the fact that the government has not accepted the unanimous recommendation of the special joint committee with respect to the dropout provision. As members of the committee know, we wrestled with this problem and for a considerable time we discussed two different ways of dealing with it. One way was by providing some special category, such as for students, firefighters and other groups. The other way was by increasing the dropout provision.
The members of the joint committee know that I went along with the argument advanced by the supporters of the government, and I think advanced by the staff people we had before us, to the effect that setting up special categories would not be a good idea. But I went along with that proposition because of the agreement that was reached to recommend a dropout of 20 per cent rather than 10 per cent. It is a matter of knowledge among those of us who were there that there was a certain amount of bargaining all the way from 10 per cent to 25 per cent; but in the end we agreed on 20 per cent, on the understanding that no member of the committee would vote against it. I do not think

that even the time honoured words "on division" were used when this figure was arrived at. Therefore I am quite disappointed that the minister now tells us that the government has decided to recommend a change to 15 per cent only rather than to 20 per cent.
As others have pointed out, the 10 per cent dropout provision made possible dropping out only 4.7 years out of the 47 of a full working career. In our recommendation that the figure be 20 per cent we would have provided for 9.4 years. Even that figure did not cover some cases which were brought to us, but I for one felt that that was a reasonable figure and made possible staying in school up to age 25 and dropping out certain other years of low income. I felt that those who stayed at school to get a better education were the people who would not need many dropout years, so I felt that the 20 per cent figure or the 9.4 years dropout was a reasonable one and that the committee was doing a reasonable thing in settling for that on a unanimous basis.
This proposal for a 15 per cent dropout puts this back to only 7.05 years that can be dropped out of the calculation so far as lifetime earnings are concerned. As has already been said, Mr. Chairman, this leaves no margin for people who may stay in school until 25 years of age, and it will create other problems. As a matter of fact, what is going to happen is that people who want to receive special consideration in respect of special categories will again raise their voices. I hope the government will yet reconsider this whole question and go along with what was recommended unanimously by the committee.
A great deal has been said during our discussions about the good work that was done by the committee. The committee has been commended for its attendance, study and attention to the briefs, and has been commended for its recommendations, and up to this point all of the recommendations have been accepted. I am quite disappointed that this unanimous recommendation has not been concurred in by the government.
I made a few notes while the minister was speaking as to what I might say, and I discover that one of them relates to a point already made by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, but perhaps I may be allowed to repeat it. If the minister contends that this provision can be changed 10 or 20 years from now, why put in any figure at this time? Why not just leave it to some future and wiser parliament, as the minister would say, to wrestle with this problem?
Canada Pension Plan
The fact of the matter is that by putting in a figure now we are telling the Canadian people that this is the structure of this bill, and I am sure this will be disappointing, particularly in view of the fact there has been public knowledge of the unanimous agreement of the committee regarding the 20 per cent figure. There will be disappointment in respect of the government's decision that the figure should be set at 15 per cent.
Mr. Chairman, we should reconsider this situation, and therefore I have written out an amendment to the amendment which I propose to move. I point out to you, sir, and to all members of this committee, that the minister's amendment has been brought in without any prior resolution, and therefore it is not regarded as one which is contrary to the general terms of the plan. Her amendment is one that cannot be ruled out for the reasons some of us advanced last night against another amendment. It is my submission that if the minister has the right to move a change from 10 per cent to 15 per cent without a prior resolution it is my right as a member of this committee to move a further change from 15 per cent to 20 per cent.

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. Without questioning or going into the submission with respect to the resolution, which perhaps could be contended as not being applicable in this particular case, the hon. member's amendment will create a

Canada Pension Plan
charge on the consolidated revenue fund. The minister read the figures in this regard, which indicate that many millions of dollars would be involved. All taxes, duties and grants of money, and all measures imposing financial burdens on the people are matters within the sole jurisdiction of the House of Commons.

The principle that the sanction of the crown must be given to every grant of money drawn from the public revenue, applies equally to the taxation levied to provide that revenue.

Mr. Chairman, I think to follow the argument of the parliamentary secretary would be to carry the ruling Your Honour made last night to its final and ultimate extreme. We are inclined to agree with the proposition put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. He would not agree with us last night but he is agreeing with us today, and I suppose better late than never. On that ground we are going to support his proposition that this particular amendment is in order.
I merely want to put it this way. If Your Honour should follow the proposition put forward by the parliamentary secretary, then any amendment whatever to this bill that any private member might put forward, which would in any way affect the contributions to be made, the benefits to be paid out, the period during which contributions would be accepted, the age of persons entitled to benefits, the conditions under which they would benefit-anything down to the most minute and minor change in the bill- would be assumed to be a charge on the public or to be a change in the plan and therefore out of order. I cannot see that such a ruling could be made on a bill of the magnitude of this one, and that the only amendments to the bill that can be put forward are amendments proposed by the government.
The sequence of the argument put forward by the parliamentary secretary is that an amendment to the dropout period would make some pensions a little better, that therefore there might be more money paid out of the fund, that therefore there would be a charge on the revenue and the minister should bring this in by way of resolution, or else it is out of order. This is the logical sequence of his argument. To what point of absurdity can one go in a ruling of this type?
I say that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is in order and we intend to support it because it is restoring what the joint committee recommended. For that reason we say that to follow the argument of the parliamentary secretary would be to carry your ruling to the point of absurdity. No, Mr. Chairman, I should like to speak to this subamendment. We know that this subamendment will correct some inequities that would be facing students in Canada. We are aware that the minister's amendment leaves this at 15 per cent.
Since the minister has introduced the matter by mentioning the brief received from the Canadian students union, I think this is a good time to emphasize the students' claims with respect to this legislation. Students who take advanced training, which may well go beyond the age of 25, will be badly hit by this bill. Just for the purposes of dropout during the time they are at university they would need seven years, and if we allowed a 20 per cent dropout they would require another two years on top of that because, after they leave university and enter the labour market, they generally have low earnings during their first two years of employment. At the other end of the scale, if they stop work at an early age, as often happens, they will not have enough dropout years.
It might be argued that this is a specific case and does not merit great consideration. I deny that, because though this parliament is not specifically interested in dealing with education, that being a matter for the provinces, nevertheless we should not discourage students from going to university, and in effect that is what this limited dropout provision will do.
A far better solution would be to allow students to drop out the years which they attend university, and I hope to move an amendment toward that end when we reach the next clause.

Canada Pension Plan
We need highly skilled and educated people in Canada. We are hearing more and more about the effects of automation, and more and more about unemployment, particularly from the Minister of Labour. That is also a strong argument not to discriminate in this manner against students who are taking advanced training.
The minister referred to the students brief as a particularly good one. In it they urged that the most satisfactory way of curing the problem would be through the method which I hope to propose in my amendment, and at this point I would like to emphasize some of the arguments presented by the students.
First, they pointed out that students' expenses have increased substantially in recent years, that tuition fees have gone up, that room and board are more expensive than they used to be, and that all other living expenses have risen correspondingly. This means students require more money.
Some of them go to work in the summertime. In fact in my area in Saskatchewan every student who can find a job does go to work in the summer, but summer earnings have not kept pace with what I might call the rising cost of university living. Not only that, but there is a depreciating number of jobs. This is not to say that the absolute number of jobs has declined, but because university enrolment is rising so rapidly job opportunities are not rising at the same rate, and hence more and more students find they are unable to get summer jobs. Even when they do, they have to take lower wages than were offered a few years ago, due to the pressure on the labour market.
The University of Victoria which investigated this problem found that 8,000 of its students did not find jobs in 1961-62. It also found that 13.4 per cent of the students were unemployed in the summer of 1963, and that 26.5 per cent had employment for only part of the summer. This emphasizes the point that it is essential we should not discourage students by making them use their university years as dropout years. The University of Victoria also noted that their average earnings were something like $595; and if that is so, then obviously they would have to use their university years as dropout years. It is correct some did make more than that, in fact as much as $1,500, but generally speaking their incomes were relatively low.
These are some of the arguments which make me feel it is important that students should not be penalized by having a 15 per

cent dropout provision instead of a 20 per cent figure. In fact, I believe students should be allowed to have their university years excluded from the dropout provision.

I am very disappointed with the attitude of the minister. The special joint committee was unanimous in recommending a 20 per cent dropout. In fact this was a compromise by committee members. The Ontario recommendation was that the pension should be calculated on the basis of the best 10 years of earnings, or perhaps the last 10 years of earnings, and personally that is what I favour; but for the sake of unanimity our group on the committee went along with the 20 per cent compromise even though we preferred a dropout of 25 per cent.
I wish to endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Kindersley. In the report by Dr. John Deutsch of the economic council it has been pointed out that Canada is 20 years behind the United States in technological and scientific skill, and we have seen newspaper reports of highly trained and skilled Canadians leaving the country.
Canada should do everything in its power to encourage attendance at university, and it is essential that the government reconsider its stand and adopt the 20 per cent dropout recommended by the joint committee. However, judging by the attitude of hon. members on the other side, they are not considering the interests of university students and will vote against the amendment which we shall move later.
I now want to make a plea for the married women of Canada, those who stay at home and attend to their families and children. The Canada pension plan penalizes them, and this reduction in the dropout from 20 per cent to 15 per cent further discriminates against them. I shall give an example. A young lady who starts working at age 20 may work for five years with average earnings of $2,500 a year. She does not return to the labour market and at age 65 she will be offered the generous pension of $6.17 a month. If she had taken her pension plan contributions and bought herself an annuity from the government she could have a pension of $16.20 a month.
I shall give another example, of a young lady starting work at 20, who works for ten years and has average earnings of $3,000. She then stays at home attending to her family and at age 65 she will get the magnificent pension of $15.43 a month. If she

took her pension contributions and invested in a government annuity she could have a pension of $40 a month. If the dropout had been 20 per cent, at least there would have been some adjustment-it would not have been a major one-in favour of that type of woman. But no, Mr. Chairman, obviously the government is not concerned with the woman who stays at home and minds her children; and I am surprised that the minister, one of the same fair sex, does what she does.
The next point I want to make with regard to this dropout provision is that I think it is generally agreed that people in the higher income brackets, say $5,000 a year or more, have a continuity, generally, in their employment. It is the people in the lower income brackets whose employment record is erratic; they are the ones who for many years perhaps earn less than the minimum provided for in the bill. Therefore I maintain that reducing the dropout penalizes the people in the lower income brackets. Of course, the Canada pension plan does that throughout, but at least in this one respect, with regard to the dropout, certainly the government should consider that increasing the dropout provision penalizes those people in the lower income brackets, because they are the ones who have the erratic employment record.
I am surprised that the minister now, all of a sudden, is very concerned that at some particular point in history there will be a drain on the fund greater than they had anticipated. I submit that students are not a group or class of people in that sense. Students, according to the definition we usually accept, are people who are taking post-secondary education at a vocational school, a university or in any other type of full-time academic work. Students are not confined to a certain type or class of person according to income and we want to exempt them across the board. At any time up to the age of 25 a student who is attending a university full time would be able to exclude those years from the calculations under the Canada pension plan. As has been explained, the pension is payable on 25 per cent of the average lifetime earnings of any person under this act.
In the case of students who attend a university or vocational school until the age of 25, now that we have accepted 15 per cent, which gives them only seven years during which their earnings can be dropped out from their average, they are not given one more year from the time they become 25 until they retire at 65. In other words, for 40 years they must pay into the Canada pension plan. If they are sick and off for a year, if they suffer any disability or if they are unemployed or anything else happens to them during that period of 40 years, their average earnings come down. Believe me, the total is not great. The maximum pension at the moment is $104 per month. If you do not make an exception for students, then every year during that 40 years will bring down their average and bring down the pension they have earned.
We believe that the figure of 15 per cent, or even 20 per cent as proposed by the joint committee, does not meet the position of students whom members of parliament and of the legislatures and many of our social and economic organizations throughout Canada have been encouraging to continue their education either at a vocational school or a university. Mr. Chairman, last week one of the hon. members opposite drew the committee's attention to a situation which will occur in 1968 and 1969 involving widows in receipt of widow's pension who reach the age of 65 during one of those two years. A widow in receipt of a pension calculated at $25 a month plus 37J per cent of her husband's retirement pension who becomes 65 at any time between February 1, 1968 and November 30, 1969, would suffer a temporary drop in the size of her pension income for a period not exceeding 12 months. When she reaches age 65, the widow's pension changes from the flat rate $25 plus 37J per cent to an amount equal to 60 per cent of her husband's retirement pension. For any widow this will entail a decrease in the amount of the widow's pension. For most widows, this difference will be more than made up by the availability of the $75 a month old age security pension at age 65. However, in the years 1968 and 1969, old age security will not yet be available to widows on reaching their 65th birthday.
A widow who reaches age 65 in 1968 will suffer a drop in her widow's pension following her 65th birthday, and will not be able to receive her $75 old age security pension until she reaches age 66, some time during 1969. For 12 months, then, she will have to take a lower pension.

The widow who reaches the age 65 some time in 1969 will similarly suffer a drop in her widow's pension, and will be unable to claim her $75 old age security pension until January 1, 1970. She will therefore receive a reduced pension for something less than 12 months.
It was suggested the government give consideration to meeting this situation. After due consideration, the government is prepared to propose adding a new subclause (6) to clause

Canada Pension Plan
58. It provides that a widow can receive either the basic monthly amount of the pension as set forth in paragraph (a) of subclause (1) of clause 56 or the basic amount referred to in paragraph (b) of subclause (1) of clause 56, whichever is the greater. This alternative will be open only to those widows who reach age 65 during the calendar years 1968 or 1969, having already become entitled to a widow's pension before reaching that age. This alternative will be open to such a widow only for a month during which no retirement pension can be paid to such a person because of her age as set forth in clause 56. It is important to recognize that some widows will become entitled to retirement pensions in their own right on reaching age 65. The amount of the retirement pension has a direct effect on the amount of the widow's pension as provided in subclause (2) of clause 56. The special arrangement contemplated by this new subclause (6) of clause 56 is therefore designed to apply only during a period when such a widow cannot yet claim a retirement pension because she has not reached the age specified in clause 66 at which a retirement pension could be paid to her. In this regard, the fact that she may not have contributed toward a retirement pension in her own right does not alter the general rule.
The practical end result of this proposal is that, during the years 1968 and 1969 only, until a widow can apply for her $75 old age security pension, and an earnings related retirement pension, she may continue to receive the $25 a month flat rate pension plus 37\ per cent of her husband's retirement pension since this amounts to more than the 60 per cent figure to which she would normally be entitled under subparagraph (b) of subclause (1).
The amendment that will be moved by the Minister of National Revenue is as follows:
That clause 56 be amended by adding thereto the following subclause:
(6) Where a widow reaches 65 years of age in 1968 or 1969 after a widow's pension has become payable to her, the monthly amount of such pension for any months in those years after she reaches that age but for which by virtue of section 66 no retirement pension is payable under this act to a person of her age shall be calculated as though for the reference in paragraph (b) of subsection (1) of this section to the basic monthly amount mentioned therein, there were substituted a reference to the greater of that basic monthly amount or the basic monthly amount of the widow's pension payable to her immediately before she reached 65 years of age.
